Name: Black Swan
Review: An absolute masterclass in the psychological horror genre. Just as a dancer is required to play the perfect swan queen, Natalie Portman plays both roles of Nina's white side and eventually unlocked dark side as she further slips into psychosis. An Oscar well deserved. What I love the most about perfectly executed films like this is when the playing field isn't even as large as you think it is. All Darren Aronofsky needs is Nina's mind, and everything falls into place. The use of body horror and her descent into madness leaves the viewer questioning what is real or what is merely an illusion, and a reflection on her current state. Every mirror becomes something you fear, and every physical toll she endures acts as a visual representation of her fracturing mind. But most of all, it demonstrates the agonizing pursuit of perfection, and the cost she pays to achieve what she believes others cannot.

Name: Se7en
Review: Incredible performances from Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman. Easily Fincher's second best plot twist, (obviously below something I shouldn't talk about). The contrast in character between these two build a magnificent foundation for the ultimate philosophical climax. For anyone against the pacing: develop an attention span. No one is going to appreciate Mills and Somerset as a duo with remotely the same potency if there aren't any slower scenes that allows a development in their relationship or their own individual character arcs. We aren't watching Tom and Jerry, so just shut up and let the film play itself out. What I loved about this the most that constantly delivered in every scene was the setting. The perpetual rain in the city, the use of darkness, even the crimes scenes all evoked decay and vulnerability in the viewer during those key moments.

Name: Uncut Gems
Review: Man, what a ride. I had no idea Adam Sandler had this potential to play such a serious role so excellently. If you gamble big and lose, your life is over. If you gamble big and you succeed, you win big. However, do you really win big in the long run?
